set.description: Acre is a resort and farm in San José del Cabo. Its restaurant holds a Michelin Green Star. In the empty center of a circular permaculture garden, the owners were running an open-fire dinner as a pop-up: private buyouts, winemaker dinners, a dark sky above. They called it Rústico. The season was starting and it needed a brand. Cam Watt, the owner, wrote the brief himself: "We want to create an 'experience' or a 'memory'."

children.text: His worry was obviousness. "Avoid anything too obvious or predictable. Simple and clear always works for me." Acre already had a brand and a whole family of things under it: a bar, the restaurant, weddings, treehouses. Rústico had to read as Acre's, the baby brother of a bigger restaurant to come, without competing with the reputation next door. A place like that cannot out-shout its setting. It has to disappear into it.

We showed several routes. Cam liked the burgundy in one; we recommended the structure of another with that color. He answered: "I trust you." The idea is a circle: seed, harvest, fire, table, community. A wordmark set in Forevs lifts the dinner from casual to ceremonial. A hand-led second logotype keeps the farm in it. Mulled wine, fired brick, terracotta and white linen: firelight in the field, soil underfoot.

Brand strategy and essence, the identity system and a brand book: primary and secondary logotypes, the "by Acre" lockup, color, Maison Neue with Caslon Ionic, a set of stamps, headline frames cut like flame, photography rules and social templates. Logo files and graphic elements, ready for the sign Cam needed right away.

Paolo Vincenti, co-owner: "We consider this approved." Rústico runs under the name, and Acre kept a page of its own for it because, in their words, it is new. The work grew into a brand manual for the whole resort, which the owners said they had been missing for some time.

set.description: A heritage leather house from Upstate New York, rebuilt for the way it sells today.

children.text: Hanks has made full-grain leather belts in Endicott, New York since 1949. Made in the USA, with a guarantee measured in generations. The business sells online only, most of it on a phone. Almost every customer was a man. The company wanted to be known for women's accessories too, and the old identity, an uppercase HANKS inside a Circle-H, had nothing to say to them.

Mia Calleo, who runs Hanks, asked for a light touch: keep the name written out, change the font, keep the H. The question underneath was harder. How does a brand built for one audience make room for another without losing the first? Our first round leaned western and the client said so: too much cowboy, not enough accessory. Men's and women's goods needed one house with a door for each.

We kept the structure of the wordmark and reset it in a serif, Proxima Sera, with a monogram H marked EST 1949. The work that mattered was the palette. A saddle-brown core for everything Hanks, then secondary families: Tanned Oak and Raw Umber for men's pieces, Forged Teal and Washed Patina for women's. Photography moved away from the ranch. The client fixed the tagline herself: crafted in America, not just designed here.

Brand guidelines: tone of voice, mission, values, the logo system, color, type, photography and social templates. A logo package in every colorway. Website design in Figma for home, category and product pages, phone first, handed to their in-house developer to build.

Mia asked for the book to feel warmer and more welcoming than "male centric", and it was revised at once. Zach Duncan, the marketing partner who brought Hanks to us, said it plainly: "the brand redesign, I'm very happy with that on the hanks. You guys did a good job."

set.description: A name and a house of color for a kids' creative space in Monterrey.

children.text: The founders, industrial designers in San Pedro Garza García, were turning a white warehouse into a place for children and families: art workshops, free play, a library, a shop and a café under one roof. They had a working name, The Lab, and one firm belief: art is a process, not a result. They needed a name and a brand before the space existed.

The hard part was the market, not the logo. Families there are used to structured entertainment and immediate results. The founders wanted to teach the value of free play and of paint on the floor, "where every stain of paint is a win." The identity also had to hold both audiences in one room: children at the tables and parents with a good coffee.

We showed directions: Playful Curiosity, geometric shapes that become characters, and Wholesome Imagination, storybook illustration. Laura Díaz de León chose the first: easy to keep in your head. The name came after the direction: Casa Colora, the house of color. A logotype a little disorganized and still balanced, a house-shaped seal, and stickers of clouds, hearts, hands and houses, drawn fat, like clay or shapes cut by small hands. Brown for the type, so beige and stickers never read as babyish.

Naming. Logotype in vertical and horizontal versions, the house seal, a palette of Soft Cream, Vivid Clay, Electric Azure, Dusty Rose, Sky Breeze and Muted Sage, Dunbar Tall with Galano Grotesque, the sticker graphics, photography direction, signage, cups, cards, a calendar and an Instagram system, all in a brand book.

set.description: A quiet-luxury identity for a stylist who dresses founders.

children.text: Rinske Fris styles male founders and executives, individually and online. Her clients are men whose businesses matured faster than their wardrobes. She had no logo, a website she barely used, and a styling app that accepts only a logo, a few colors and Google fonts. She found Atla through our content: "I feel like your messaging is so strong and I really like your feeling for design."

In her words, the service "solves the disconnect between how someone feels internally and how they show up visually." The market was the problem. Fast content, AI styling apps and generic influencers had filled the space with meaningless advice, so the depth in her work was hard to see. She wanted luxury, but "not Dubai-Loro Piana-luxury." Personal, a bit fun, calm. Her one word for the brand: alignment.

We drew moodboards: Structured Ease and Timeless Confidence. She chose the second. Quiet luxury that earns attention instead of demanding it. Refinement, not reinvention. Deep olive over ivory, with gold and brown. A stacked wordmark under the line Intentional Style, a monogram, a family of badges. Miller Display and Miller Text with League Spartan: the kind of serif she had pointed to in the moodboard.

Primary and secondary wordmarks, monogram and favicon, palette, typography, badge families, photography guidelines, an Instagram profile, post and story system, a brand guidelines book, and a newsletter template built in Flodesk.
Rinske, seeing the old and the new side by side: "now I'm like, what was I doing?" The next morning: "Very happy with the brand direction." Her newsletters have carried the olive wordmark since.

set.description: A new vitamin brand for women, named, drawn and packed before its first order.

children.text: Persona Nutrition has sold personalized vitamin packs for years to an older customer, in a clinical, evidence-first voice. Jason Brown, its co-founder and CEO, wanted a second brand for younger women: non-medical, fun, built around wellness. There was no name he liked, an internal team already drawing looks, and a launch date set for the end of the year. He wanted an outside eye.

The problem was a brand that had never spoken to this customer. Persona's language was cold on purpose. The new one had to sound like a friend who knows her supplements and never makes you feel behind. And it could not look like a pill. Vyv sells daily packs, personalized, morning and night. Every image had to say pack, not capsule.

Jason sent a shortlist. We ranked Vyv first: short, modern, a real brand, with room to grow past vitamins. Of the directions we showed, he chose the one we called supplements that embrace you: sunset colors, curves, a happy brand. The logo is lowercase vyv built from a repeated triangle. Read it again and a woman appears in the middle. Expansive radial gradients spread from the center, for vitality.

Naming input and moodboards. Logo, logotype and a 3D mark. Brand guidelines with photography rules and Instagram formats. The gradient system as editable files. Packaging: the shipping box and the large and small dispenser boxes, in lilac and maroon, print-ready. The onboarding questionnaire. The homepage, desktop and mobile, handed to their developers.

Jason, after the guidelines: "I think it's amazing, keeping it both feminine, but also a strong color palette. I love the way the logo has developed." And later: "complete different energy than I would've ever expected for this brand." Vyv launched in January 2026. The next project was Persona itself.
